paras: The attempted lynching of Wade Bennett took place on the night of Monday, December 14, 1903, when an armed mob surrounded the jail at Clayton, Georgia, intending to lynch Bennett, a Black man accused of fatally shooting a white railroad construction boss, Frank Lesuer. The jailor slipped Bennett out of the jail to a private home, where he was guarded until the mob dispersed. Only the Savannah Morning News reported the mob; other white papers carried the shooting under the headline "Lesuer Killed by Negro" without mentioning it.

Frank Lesuer was a boss for Carpenter Bros., contractors building the Tallulah Falls railroad, about 16 miles from Tallulah Falls and near Clayton. According to the Clayton Tribune, on Sunday afternoon, December 13, a dispute arose at the company's camps near Bethel church between Bennett, known about the camps as "Booze," and another white employee, and Lesuer was called on to settle it. Lesuer was shot at very short range with a single-barrel shotgun, which left a wound about three inches across below the center of the abdomen. He died at six o'clock the next morning, and he was buried at Bethel on Tuesday.

Bennett was captured about sunset on Sunday on the high trestle at Tallulah Falls as he was about to board a train. A Tallulah Falls dispatch dated December 14 placed him in the guard house there, and the Clayton Tribune said he was lodged in the jail at Clayton on Monday night. That same night, according to the Savannah Morning News, an armed mob surrounded the Clayton jail "for the purpose of lynching" him. The jailor, whom the paper called "too crafty for the would-be-lynchers," got Bennett out of the jail and into the home of a citizen, where he was kept under guard until the mob broke up.

No report of arrests of mob members, or of an indictment or trial of Bennett, was found in the coverage. In late January 1904, Lesuer's body was exhumed and shipped to "Boliver, N. Y.," reportedly at the order and expense of an Atlanta woman to whom he had been engaged.

The episode was covered only by white papers in Georgia and South Carolina, and no Black-press coverage has been found. A brief Tallulah Falls wire ran in the Union Times of Union, South Carolina, on December 18 and in the Atlanta Constitution on December 21 under the headline "Lesuer Killed by Negro," naming Bennett as "a negro" or "colored" and giving his nickname, with no mention of a mob. The Savannah Morning News item of December 18, headlined "Jailor Saved Him," was the only report of the siege; it called the mob "would-be-lynchers" and credited the jailor, though it also stated as fact that Bennett "shot and killed" Lesuer.

The fullest local account came from the Clayton Tribune of December 17, reprinted in the Keowee Courier of Pickens, South Carolina, on December 23. It called Bennett "the murderer," described Lesuer's wound, death and burial in detail, and said nothing about a mob at the jail. When the Keowee Courier reported the exhumation in February 1904, it again described Lesuer as "murdered by Booze Bennett" while giving no word of Bennett's fate.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Wade Bennett
bases: An armed mob surrounded the Clayton jail to lynch a Black prisoner accused of killing a white construction boss and was thwarted when the jailor hid him (A1); this is an attempted lynching.

An armed mob gathered at the jail for the purpose of lynching Bennett, an extralegal act by a group under the pretext of punishing a killing, but the jailor removed him and the mob dispersed without killing anyone (A1). No one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The shooting and Bennett's arrest are corroborated by three reports (A2, A3, A4), but the mob at the jail appears only in the Savannah Morning News (A1); the local Clayton Tribune account does not mention it (A4).

accounts.gist: Bennett and Lesuer 'engaged in a row' that ended with Lesuer shot in the abdomen; Bennett was in the guard house at Tallulah Falls. No mob is mentioned.

accounts.label: Clayton Tribune (local)
accounts.gist: Lesuer was shot while settling a dispute between Bennett and another white employee; Bennett was captured on the Tallulah Falls trestle and lodged in the Clayton jail Monday night. No mob is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined the rescue, 'Jailor Saved Him', called the mob 'would-be-lynchers' and praised the jailor as 'too crafty' for them, while stating as fact that Bennett 'shot and killed' Lesuer.
The Tallulah Falls wire ran under 'Lesuer Killed by Negro' in Union, S.C., and Atlanta, identifying Bennett by race and nickname and saying nothing of a mob.
The Clayton Tribune, reprinted in the Keowee Courier, called Bennett 'the murderer' and gave a sympathetic account of Lesuer's death and burial, without mentioning the mob.
